title: Announcement — ROSS Intelligence Shuts Down Operations
author: Andrew Arruda · Jimoh Ovbiagele · Pargles Dall'Oglio

dom.t: ROSS shutdown: Litigation can eliminate unresolved competitors

st.t: ROSS shutdown: Litigation can eliminate unresolved competitors
st.an: ROSS’s announcement directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition by attributing its shutdown to litigation-driven fundraising constraints and exhausted operating funds. It also corroborates the distinction between discontinued operations and insurance-funded litigation, while presenting exclusionary motive and future competition or access benefits as the founders’ allegations and hopes rather than adjudicated findings.
qs: With our company ensnared by this legal battle, we have been unable to raise another round of funding to fuel our development and marketing efforts.
Although we are out of funds for our operations, ROSS has insurance for our litigation costs.

kp.k: ROSS announces shutdown of its legal research platform
kp.d: The founders announce the decision to cease operations and make the platform unavailable as of January 31, 2021. The December 11, 2020 announcement states that acceptance of new customers had stopped on Monday of that week. This is a company account of its own closure, rather than evidence of industry-wide displacement or adoption trends.
qs: We have made the difficult decision to shut down operations at ROSS Intelligence.
As of Monday of this week, we have no longer been accepting new customers.
As of January 31, 2021, the ROSS platform will no longer be available.

kp.k: Founders present research innovation as an accessibility strategy
kp.d: The founders describe a six-year effort to make legal services more accessible through more efficient, less expensive legal research. They report serving large and small firms, solo practitioners, students, pro se litigants, academics and librarians, with user feedback shaping development. These are stated goals and company-reported activities; the announcement supplies no quantified efficiency, cost or access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: Six years ago, we set out to make legal services more accessible by innovating legal research.
We felt then, as we do today, that legal research could be more efficient, less expensive, and more accessible.
At every turn, we’ve been grateful to receive lawyers’ and other legal researchers’ feedback to shape ROSS’s development.

We’ve been honored to serve legal researchers in many contexts across the U.S.: lawyers in large firms and small firms; solo practitioners; students; pro se litigants; academics; librarians; and more.

kp.k: Founders attribute closure to litigation and blocked fundraising
kp.d: The founders attribute the shutdown to the burden of the lawsuit brought by Thomson Reuters and Westlaw in spring 2020, saying the legal battle prevented another funding round for development and marketing and left operating funds running out. Their characterization of the suit as strategically intended to burden ROSS is an allegation by a litigating party, not a judicial finding reported in the announcement.
qs: However, just as Westlaw devised it to be, this ongoing suit has been heavy for ROSS to bear.
With our company ensnared by this legal battle, we have been unable to raise another round of funding to fuel our development and marketing efforts.
Our bank account is running out, and we must cease operations in the New Year.

kp.k: Shutdown entails data export and migration to competing platforms
kp.d: ROSS commits to maintaining service until January 31, 2021, enabling customers to export personal and saved-folder data beginning in January, and helping customers transition to services including Fastcase, vLex and Casetext. These are announced transition arrangements, not reported completed migrations.
qs: ROSS will continue to be available as it is today until January 31, 2021.
Each customer will be able to export their personal data, including all data from their saved folders, beginning in January.
We will be working with our customers to transition them to other services — including platforms by our friends at Fastcase, vLex and Casetext.

kp.k: Insurance enables continued litigation despite operational closure
kp.d: The founders distinguish the end of platform operations from the continuation of the company for litigation: they state that insurance covers litigation costs despite exhausted operating funds. They frame continued litigation as pursuing access to justice and resisting alleged suppression of competition, and express the hope—not an established outcome—that the case’s precedent will encourage innovation.
qs: We have not abandoned our vision for access to justice through the use of technology.
However, we are now pursuing that vision in the courthouse rather than the marketplace.
Although we are out of funds for our operations, ROSS has insurance for our litigation costs.

The company will continue as a going concern so that the facts at the heart of this lawsuit are brought to light and so that Westlaw’s tactics — using litigation as a weapon and stifling competition — do not succeed.
We hope that by continuing in this way, the precedent this court case sets will inspire innovation rather than shut down competition.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The ROSS founders present technology-enabled legal research as a route to greater efficiency, lower expense and accessibility, while claiming that their work already made research tasks more efficient.
pts.d: Andrew Arruda, Jimoh Ovbiagele and Pargles Dall’Oglio, signing as the founders with the ROSS team, describe improved legal research as their means of making legal services more accessible. They claim practical efficiency improvements but express lower costs and broader accessibility as a continuing vision rather than quantified outcomes. The announcement does not isolate AI's contribution or describe particular AI capabilities.

pts.k: The founders attribute ROSS's operational shutdown to litigation-related funding constraints and frame the dispute as a threat to innovation and competition in legal research.
pts.d: The founders say the ongoing lawsuit prevented another funding round, leaving insufficient funds for operations, development and marketing. Their characterization of Westlaw as using litigation to suppress competition is their allegation, not an established finding reported in the announcement. They express hope, rather than a firm prediction, that continuing the litigation will produce a precedent supportive of innovation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The announcement relies on the founders' experience developing and operating ROSS, customer feedback and their account of the company's financial position.
pts.d: For product benefits, the founders cite work with partners and feedback from legal researchers, without providing research-time measurements, cost comparisons, benchmarks or measured access-to-justice outcomes. For the shutdown, they offer a firsthand account of fundraising failure and dwindling funds. Linked reporting concerns the lawsuit, but the announcement supplies no independent financial documentation or adjudicated finding establishing the alleged anticompetitive intent.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The December 11, 2020 announcement looks back over six years of development and schedules platform closure for January 31, 2021.
pts.d: The founders describe their accessibility and efficiency ambitions as continuing from the company's beginnings through the announcement. New-customer intake had stopped on the Monday of the announcement week. Existing customers would retain access during the transition, with personal-data exports beginning in January. Continued litigation, unlike continued product operations, was supported by insurance; no date or assured outcome was given for the hoped-for precedent.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected users span US legal researchers in firms, independent practice, education and self-representation; existing customers must migrate to other services.
pts.d: The founders identify lawyers in large and small firms, solo practitioners, students, pro se litigants, academics and librarians as users served. These customers face the loss of the ROSS platform and a transition to alternatives, with data export and migration assistance promised. The broader public is an intended beneficiary of the access-to-justice vision, but the announcement does not demonstrate reductions in unmet legal need. The founders also frame other innovators and competitors in legal research as potentially affected by the litigation's precedent. ROSS is discussed as a legal-research product provider, not as an ALSP delivering legal work.
